rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Velocity is frame-dependent: the relative velocity of A with respect to B is the vector difference $\vec v_{AB} = \vec v_A - \vec v_B$. Same-direction motion subtracts speeds (20 and 25 m/s give 5 m/s — NEB 2017); opposite-direction motion adds them; angled motion needs the cosine rule.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - v_AB = v_A − v_B - Same direction: v_rel = |v_A − v_B|; opposite: v_rel = v_A + v_B - Rain-umbrella: tan θ = v_p/v_r

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Vector Subtraction Rule:** $\vec{v}_{B/A} = \vec{v}_B - \vec{v}_A$ is the velocity of B as measured in A's rest frame. The order matters: $\vec{v}_{A/B} = -\vec{v}_{B/A}$. This is a vector equation — subtract components, not speeds.  ·  **Galilean Relativity Limit:** Velocity addition $\vec{v} = \vec{v}' + \vec{u}$ (where $\vec{u}$ is frame velocity) is valid only for speeds $\ll c$. At relativistic speeds, Einstein's velocity addition $v = (v' + u)/(1 + v'u/c^2)$ must be used. For everyday kinematics, Galilean addition is exact.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "There is no absolute rest — only frames."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***20 m/s and 25 m/s same direction*** — relative velocity 5 m/s (NEB 2017).

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **v_AB vs v_BA:** v_AB = v_A − v_B (A seen from B); v_BA is its negative — same magnitude, opposite direction.  ·  **Relative speed in same vs opposite direction:** same direction subtracts; opposite directions add.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Motion Depends on Who Is Watching A passenger walking forward at 1 m/s in a train moving at 20 m/s moves at 21 m/s relative to the ground but 1 m/s relative to the train. Velocity has meaning only **relative to a frame** — this topic defines relative velocity and works the standard cases: same direction, opposite direction, perpendicular crossing (rain-umbrella, boat-river).  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2017) **Relative velocity:** the velocity of body A as observed from body B: $$\vec v_{AB} = \vec v_A - \vec v_B$$ (velocity of A minus velocity of B, vector subtraction). | Case | Relative velocity | |---|---| | Same direction | $v_{AB} = v_A - v_B$ (difference of magnitudes) | | Opposite directions | $v_{AB} = v_A + v_B$ (sum of magnitudes) | | At angle θ | magnitude $\sqrt{v_A^2 +…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Same direction minus, opposite plus, angled — cosine rule."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (3m): A river 200 m wide flows at 3 m/s; a boat aimed straight across moves at 4 m/s. Find crossing time and downstream drift.** — t = 200/4 = 50 s; drift = 3 × 50 = 150 m; resultant speed 5 m/s at 36.9° from straight-across.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Most-tested: the definition + same-direction numerical (2017). Boat-river and rain-umbrella are the classic extension problems.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **All velocity is relative:** stating a velocity without naming the frame is incomplete — the ground frame is just a convention.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: v_AB = v_A − v_B (vector subtraction).  ·  Same direction: difference of speeds; opposite: sum; angle θ: √(v_A² + v_B² − 2v_Av_B cos θ).  ·  Rain-umbrella: tan θ = v_person/v_rain, tilt forward. Boat-river: aim straight → drift = v_river × t.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Aeroplane timetables account for jet streams — the same aircraft flies Kathmandu–Doha faster westward-to-eastward because the wind is a relative-velocity term.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 3. Worked Numericals **Q1:** A boat crosses a 200 m river, current 3 m/s, boat speed 4 m/s in still water, aimed straight across. Find crossing time and drift. *Crossing time:* t = width/$v_{boat}$ = 200/4 = 50 s. *Drift:* = $v_{river} \times t$ = 3 × 50 = 150 m downstream. *Resultant velocity:* $\sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5$ m/s at $\tan^{-1}(3/4) = 36.9°$ from straight-across.…  ·  ## 4. Conceptual Relationships - **To Topic 6:** relative velocity is velocity defined against a moving frame — same derivative idea, different reference. - **To Vectors:** relative velocity is vector subtraction — the magnitude formula mirrors the cosine rule.…  ·  ## 5. rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Apparent vs Real Motion:** In the rain/river problems, the actual velocity of the rain/boat is unchanged; only the *observed* (relative) velocity changes when the observer moves. The rain still falls vertically; the umbrella is tilted to match the apparent velocity.  ·  Verified PYQ: define relative velocity + two-car numerical (2017, 2m).  ·  Why does rain appear slanted to a moving observer?
